description: How 1688 ended Catholic monarchy and established a constitutional settlement Parliament could defend.
content_html:
James II and the Crisis of 1688

Charles II (restored 1660) was a pragmatic ruler who avoided a direct collision with Parliament. His brother James II (king 1685–1688) was not. James was openly Catholic and determined to use royal prerogative to promote Catholic interests: he suspended the penal laws against Catholics and Dissenters using his Dispensing Power, placed Catholics in military command posts, and in June 1688 ordered the Church of England to read his Declaration of Indulgence from every pulpit. Seven bishops who refused were arrested and tried for seditious libel — but the jury acquitted them on 30 June 1688.

On the same day as the bishops’ acquittal, seven prominent Englishmen — Whig and Tory, lords and bishops — wrote to William of Orange, the Dutch Protestant stadtholder, inviting him to bring an army to England. Their letter cited James’s violations of English law and the Protestant religion. William landed at Torbay in November 1688. James’s army disintegrated, James fled to France, and Parliament declared that he had “abdicated”.

Key Fact

Three actions by James II triggered the Glorious Revolution: his use of the Dispensing Power to suspend anti-Catholic laws without Parliament; his appointment of Catholics to military commands; and his order that the Church of England read his Declaration of Indulgence from pulpits. The trial and acquittal of the Seven Bishops showed that even the judiciary would not support him.

The Bill of Rights 1689

William III and Mary II were crowned jointly in April 1689 after accepting the Bill of Rights. This was not a modern-style declaration of individual rights but a constitutional document that listed what the crown could no longer do without parliamentary consent. The Bill of Rights:

  • Banned the suspension of laws without parliamentary consent
  • Banned the maintenance of a standing army in peacetime without Parliament’s approval
  • Required free elections for MPs and free speech inside Parliament
  • Required regular Parliaments

Alongside the Bill of Rights came the Toleration Act (1689), which allowed Protestant Dissenters to worship freely. Catholics were specifically excluded from its protections, and the Act of Settlement (1701) barred Catholics from the throne entirely. The Glorious Revolution was, in this sense, a Protestant settlement — its benefits were primarily for Anglican and Dissenting Protestants, not all subjects.

The term “Glorious Revolution” was coined by Protestants who saw 1688 as a bloodless, providential deliverance from Catholic tyranny. This framing needs critical examination. James II’s flight, not a formal battle, explains the lack of English bloodshed — but William’s campaign involved real violence in Ireland (the Williamite Wars of 1689–91) where Catholic support for James was strongest.

From a Catholic or Jacobite perspective, 1688 was not glorious — it was the violent overthrow of the legitimate king by a foreign army funded by Dutch commercial interests. The Jacobite cause (support for James and his heirs) persisted for decades, culminating in the 1715 and 1745 Jacobite rebellions. Presenting 1688 in balanced terms means acknowledging these different perspectives.

Parliamentary Monarchy in the 1700s

William III needed Parliament’s money for his wars against Louis XIV of France. He called Parliament every year, and it responded by creating the Bank of England (1694) and developing the National Debt — mechanisms that gave Parliament permanent leverage over royal finances. The Triennial Act of 1694 further regularised Parliament’s role.

The death of Queen Anne without heirs led to the Act of Union with Scotland (1707) and, via the Act of Settlement, the Hanoverian succession: George I arrived in 1714 speaking little English and heavily dependent on his ministers. Under George I and George II, Robert Walpole became effectively the first Prime Minister — holding office by managing Parliament rather than through royal favour alone. By 1750 it was clear that real executive power was shifting from the king to the ministers who commanded a parliamentary majority.

Key Fact

The Bill of Rights (1689) banned the crown from: suspending laws without Parliament; maintaining a standing army in peacetime without Parliament; interfering in elections or debate in Parliament. It also required regular Parliaments. Together these constraints ended the possibility of personal rule on the Stuart model.

Robert Walpole served as First Lord of the Treasury from 1721 to 1742 — the longest continuous tenure of any British Prime Minister. He achieved this not through royal patronage alone but by managing Parliament through a network of patronage, persuasion and political organisation. His success showed that governing Britain required parliamentary skill, not just royal favour.

Walpole’s position was a product of the 1688 settlement: a monarch dependent on parliamentary taxation needed a minister who could manage Parliament. The role of “Prime Minister” was not a formal title — Walpole himself rejected it — but it described the reality that the leader of the government’s parliamentary majority now held the real executive power.
exam_tip_html: For questions on the Glorious Revolution, be precise about what the Bill of Rights (1689) actually did — it listed specific restrictions on royal power, not a general statement of rights. Also remember that 1688 was “glorious” primarily from a Protestant perspective: the Toleration Act excluded Catholics, the Act of Settlement barred them from the throne, and the Williamite Wars caused significant bloodshed in Ireland. A strong answer will acknowledge this range of perspectives rather than simply stating that 1688 created a fair constitutional settlement for everyone.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Glorious Revolution of 1688 removed James II because he had violated the Protestant constitutional settlement — using royal prerogative to suspend laws without Parliament and promote Catholic interests.
  • The Bill of Rights (1689) permanently restricted royal power: no standing army, no suspension of laws, no interference in elections, all without parliamentary consent.
  • By 1721, Robert Walpole’s role as effective Prime Minister showed that real executive power now required managing Parliament, not just pleasing the monarch.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Bill of Rights (1689).
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: identifies a specific restriction (e.g. it banned the crown from suspending laws without parliamentary consent) AND develops it with accurate detail (e.g. this was a direct response to James II's use of the Dispensing Power to bypass anti-Catholic legislation without consulting Parliament). Secure: valid feature with limited development. Developing: vague reference to limiting royal power. Emerging: irrelevant or no attempt.

practice_questions.text: Describe two reasons why James II's actions in 1685-88 alarmed Parliament and the Church.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason. Mastering: two accurate reasons each with specific detail (e.g. James used his Dispensing Power to suspend anti-Catholic penal laws without parliamentary consent — directly violating the constitutional settlement of 1689's predecessor; he ordered the Church of England to read his Declaration of Indulgence from every pulpit — using the Church as an instrument of Catholic policy against its will). Secure: both reasons with some development. Developing: one reason well described, one vague. Emerging: vague reference to James being Catholic.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Glorious Revolution of 1688 was significant for the development of parliamentary power.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: two or more reasons with specific evidence (the Bill of Rights (1689) formally listed what the Crown could not do without Parliament — banning the suspension of laws, standing armies and interference in elections; the Act of Settlement (1701) barred Catholics from the throne, making Parliament the arbiter of succession; William III's dependence on Parliament for war funding gave Parliament permanent financial leverage; the development of Walpole's Prime Ministerial role showed that governing Britain now required parliamentary management). Secure: two reasons with some specific detail. Developing: one developed reason or two undeveloped. Emerging: describes 1688 as important without explaining why.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Glorious Revolution was not 'glorious' from all perspectives.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: two or more factors with specific evidence (from a Catholic perspective, 1688 was the violent overthrow of the legitimate king by a foreign Protestant army — the Toleration Act excluded Catholics, the Act of Settlement barred them from the throne; from an Irish perspective, the Williamite Wars of 1689-91 caused significant military violence; from a Jacobite perspective, the legitimate Stuart succession had been broken by Parliamentary decision, not constitutional right — the 1715 and 1745 rebellions reflected this). Secure: two perspectives with some specific detail. Developing: describes one alternative perspective without explaining its basis in evidence. Emerging: vague reference to some people opposing James's removal.

practice_questions.text: How far did the events of 1688-1721 establish parliamentary sovereignty as the basis of British government? [You may consider: the Bill of Rights; the Act of Settlement; the Hanoverian succession; and any other relevant factors.]
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: sustained argument addressing both the establishment of parliamentary sovereignty (Bill of Rights restrictions; Act of Settlement made Parliament the arbiter of the throne; Triennial Act regularised Parliament; Walpole's Prime Ministerial role showed real power required parliamentary management) and its limits (the monarchy was still powerful; George III would try to reassert royal influence in the 1760s-80s; constituencies were unrepresentative — 'rotten boroughs'; most people still had no vote). Overall judgement required. Secure: argues both sides with relevant evidence; some imbalance. Developing: describes the constitutional changes accurately but does not weigh the extent of parliamentary sovereignty achieved. Emerging: narrative of 1688 events without addressing the question.

practice_questions.text: Outline the main ways the Bill of Rights (1689) limited the power of the monarchy.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: three or more specific points (banned suspension of laws without Parliament; banned peacetime standing army without Parliament; required free elections and free speech in Parliament; required regular Parliaments; made James II's Catholic successor arrangements invalid). Secure: two or three relevant points with supporting detail. Developing: one or two accurate points with limited detail. Emerging: vague reference to the Bill of Rights limiting royal power.

knowledge_checks.q: Which Act of Parliament (1689) listed specific restrictions on royal power, including banning the suspension of laws without parliamentary consent?
Who became effectively Britain's first Prime Minister, serving as First Lord of the Treasury from 1721 to 1742?
The Act of _____ (1701) barred Catholics from the throne and directed the succession to the Protestant House of Hanover.
The Act of Union in _____ created the united Parliament of Great Britain, merging the English and Scottish parliaments at Westminster.
Match each Act to what it established:
right: Listed restrictions on royal power and required regular free Parliaments
Gave freedom of worship to Protestant Dissenters
Barred Catholics from the throne and set the Hanoverian succession

flashcard_questions.q: When did William of Orange land in England and what was the outcome?
flashcard_questions.a: November 1688; James II fled and William and Mary were crowned jointly in April 1689.

flashcard_questions.q: Name three things the Bill of Rights (1689) banned the Crown from doing.
flashcard_questions.a: Suspending laws, maintaining a standing army in peacetime, and interfering in elections — all without Parliament's consent.
It granted freedom of worship to Protestant Dissenters, though Catholics were excluded.

flashcard_questions.q: What did the Act of Settlement (1701) establish?
flashcard_questions.a: It barred Catholics from the throne and directed the succession to the Protestant House of Hanover.

flashcard_questions.q: When did George I arrive and why was he dependent on Parliament?
flashcard_questions.a: 1714; he spoke little English and needed parliamentary ministers to govern effectively.

flashcard_questions.q: What three actions by James II most alarmed Parliament?
flashcard_questions.a: Using the Dispensing Power to bypass anti-Catholic laws; appointing Catholics to military posts; ordering the Church to read his Declaration of Indulgence.

flashcard_questions.q: When was the Act of Union with Scotland passed?
What was the significance of the Seven Bishops' trial (1688)?
flashcard_questions.a: Their acquittal showed the judiciary would not support James II, weakening his position just as William of Orange was being invited to invade.

glossary_terms.definition: The 1689 Act of Parliament that set out the rights of Parliament and the limits of royal power — including the right to regular Parliaments, free elections and free speech in Parliament.
The 1689 Act that granted freedom of worship to Protestant Dissenters (though not Catholics), ending the most severe religious persecution of the Restoration period.
The 1701 Act of Parliament that barred Catholics from the throne and directed the succession to the Protestant House of Hanover.
The 1694 Act requiring Parliament to meet at least every three years, and limiting any Parliament to a maximum of three years — strengthening parliamentary regularity.
The parliamentary union of England and Scotland in 1707, creating Great Britain with a single Parliament at Westminster.
The Whig politician who served as First Lord of the Treasury from 1721-1742 and is often regarded as Britain's first effective Prime Minister.
